::: {.solutions}

Logarithms turn a hard equation (an unknown in the exponent, a product, a ratio) into an easy one — **as long
as you obey the laws and watch the domain**. TMUA rarely asks you to "evaluate a log". It asks you to decide
**whether a log exists**, **which way a log graph bends** for a given base, **which of several logs is
biggest**, to **rewrite** with the laws, to **substitute** so that a hidden quadratic appears, to **reject**
the impossible root, to handle a **base-flip** inequality, or to count **how many** solutions there are.
Nothing on this page uses $e$ or $\ln$ (both are outside the TMUA specification).

## When does $\log_a b$ exist?

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### 1 · Definition
$$\log_a b=c\iff a^{c}=b$$
A log is an **exponent**: "what power of $a$ gives $b$?"

[$\log_2 8=3$, $\log_9 3=\tfrac12$, $\log_{1/2}8=-3$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 2 · The three conditions
$$a>0,\qquad a\ne1,\qquad b>0$$
$a\le0$: powers are undefined or jump in sign. $a=1$: $1^{c}=1$ always. $b\le0$: $a^{c}>0$ can never reach it.

[$\log_x(5-x)$ needs $x>0,\ x\ne1,\ x<5$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 3 · The four sign cases
$$\log_a b>0\iff (a-1)(b-1)>0$$

| | $0<b<1$ | $b=1$ | $b>1$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $a>1$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $0<a<1$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

[base and argument on the **same** side of $1$ $\Rightarrow$ positive]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 4 · Bigger than 1?
$$\log_a b>1\iff\begin{cases}b>a & (a>1)\\ 0<b<a & (0<a<1)\end{cases}$$

[$\log_2 3>1$ but $\log_3 2<1$; in fact $\log_3 2=\dfrac1{\log_2 3}$]{.eg}
:::

::::

## Graphs

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### 5 · $y=\log_a x$, base above or below 1
Always: domain $x>0$, asymptote $x=0$, through $(1,0)$, $(a,1)$, $\left(\tfrac1a,-1\right)$.
$$a>1:\ \text{increasing}\qquad 0<a<1:\ \text{decreasing}$$
$$\log_{1/a}x=-\log_a x\quad(\text{reflect in the }x\text{-axis})$$
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 6 · Changing the base
$a>1$: a **bigger** base gives a **flatter** curve — for $x>1$, $\log_3 x<\log_2 x$; for $0<x<1$ the order
reverses. All the curves cross at $(1,0)$.

$y=\log_a x$ is $y=a^{x}$ reflected in $y=x$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 7 · The base as the variable
$$f(a)=\log_a b=\frac1{\log_b a}$$
Vertical asymptote at $a=1$, and $f(b)=1$. For $b>1$: $f<0$ on $0<a<1$, $f>0$ on $a>1$, decreasing on each
side. For $0<b<1$ every sign flips.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 8 · Transformations
$y=\log_a(x-p)+q$: asymptote $x=p$, domain $x>p$, through $(p+1,q)$ and $(p+a,q+1)$.

[$\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2\lvert x\rvert$ — an **even** curve on $x\ne0$]{.eg}
:::

::::

## Laws and solving

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### 9 · Laws (all arguments $>0$)
$$\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y,\qquad \log_a\tfrac{x}{y}=\log_a x-\log_a y$$
$$\log_a x^{k}=k\log_a x,\qquad a^{\log_a x}=x$$
$$\log_a b=\frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a},\quad \log_a b\cdot\log_b c=\log_a c,\quad \log_{a^{n}}b^{m}=\tfrac{m}{n}\log_a b$$
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 10 · Equations and inequalities
**Solve:** collect to one log → undo → solve → **check every argument $>0$** and every base $>0$, $\ne1$.

**Inequalities:** base $>1$ keeps the sign; base $0<a<1$ **flips** it; an unknown base means **split into
the cases** $0<x<1$ and $x>1$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 11 · Hidden quadratics
$a^{2x}$ and $a^{x}$ together: let $u=a^{x}$ and **reject $u\le0$**. $(\log x)^2$ and $\log x$ together: let
$L=\log_a x$.

[sum of the $x$-roots $=\log_a(u_1u_2)=\log_a(\text{product of the }u\text{-roots})$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### 12 · Straight-line laws
$$y=Ax^{n}\Rightarrow\log y=\log A+n\log x\quad(\log y\text{ vs }\log x)$$
$$y=Ab^{x}\Rightarrow\log y=\log A+(\log b)\,x\quad(\log y\text{ vs }x)$$
The gradient gives $n$ (or $\log b$); the intercept gives $\log A$.
:::

## Notes

### N1 · A logarithm is an exponent

$\log_a b$ answers one question: **"what power do I raise $a$ to, to get $b$?"** So
$$\log_a b=c\quad\text{means exactly}\quad a^{c}=b.$$

Read this way, most values are instant:

- $\log_2 32=5$ because $2^{5}=32$.
- $\log_9 3=\tfrac12$ because $9^{1/2}=3$.
- $\log_2\tfrac18=-3$ because $2^{-3}=\tfrac18$.
- $\log_{1/2}8=-3$ because $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{-3}=2^{3}=8$.
- $\log_a 1=0$ and $\log_a a=1$ for **every** allowed base, because $a^{0}=1$ and $a^{1}=a$.

Two facts follow straight from the definition and are used constantly:
$$a^{\log_a b}=b\qquad\text{and}\qquad\log_a\!\left(a^{c}\right)=c.$$
The log undoes the power and the power undoes the log — they are **inverse functions**.

### N2 · When does $\log_a b$ exist? — $a>0$, $a\ne1$, $b>0$

The definition asks for a power $c$ with $a^{c}=b$. Each condition rules out a case where that power either
does not exist or is not unique.

**Why the base must be positive, $a>0$.** A negative base cannot be raised to most real powers:
$(-4)^{1/2}=\sqrt{-4}$ is not a real number. Even where powers of $-2$ exist, they jump between signs
($-2,\ 4,\ -8,\ 16,\dots$), so there is no smooth curve $y=(-2)^{x}$ to invert. A zero base fails too:
$0^{c}=0$ for every $c>0$ and is undefined for $c\le0$, so $0^{c}$ can never equal, say, $5$.

**Why the base cannot be 1, $a\ne1$.** Every power of $1$ is $1$. So $\log_1 5$ asks for $1^{c}=5$, which has
**no** answer, while $\log_1 1$ asks for $1^{c}=1$, where **every** $c$ is an answer. Either way the log has no
single value.

**Why the argument must be positive, $b>0$.** Once $a>0$, every power $a^{c}$ is **strictly positive**. So
$a^{c}=0$ and $a^{c}=-4$ have no solution: $\log_2 0$ and $\log_2(-4)$ do not exist.

The existence conditions deserve a box of their own, because every later method assumes them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — the existence conditions

For $\log_a b$ to exist you need **all three**:
$$a>0,\qquad a\ne1,\qquad b>0.$$
When the base or the argument contains $x$, these three inequalities **are** the domain. Write them down
before you solve anything.
:::

Here is how the conditions turn into a domain. For $f(x)=\log_{x-1}(5-x)$:

- base positive: $x-1>0\Rightarrow x>1$;
- base not $1$: $x-1\ne1\Rightarrow x\ne2$;
- argument positive: $5-x>0\Rightarrow x<5$.

All three together give $1<x<5$ with $x\ne2$, i.e. $(1,2)\cup(2,5)$.

The same conditions also **reject roots**. Solving $\log_x 9=2$ gives $x^{2}=9$, so $x=\pm3$. A base must be
positive, so $x=-3$ is **rejected** and only $x=3$ survives.

#### Drill N2a — does it exist?

Decide whether each expression is a real number. If it is, give its value; if it is not, name the condition
that fails.

| | Expression | Exists? | Value / failed condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_{-3}9$ | | |
| (b) | $\log_1 1$ | | |
| (c) | $\log_{1/2}4$ | | |
| (d) | $\log_5 0$ | | |
| (e) | $\log_4(-16)$ | | |
| (f) | $\log_{0.3}0.09$ | | |
| (g) | $\log_{\sqrt2}\tfrac12$ | | |
| (h) | $\log_{8}2$ | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

| | Expression | Exists? | Value / failed condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_{-3}9$ | No | base $-3<0$ — even though $(-3)^2=9$, a negative base is never allowed |
| (b) | $\log_1 1$ | No | base $=1$: every power of $1$ is $1$, so there is no single answer |
| (c) | $\log_{1/2}4$ | Yes | $-2$, since $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{-2}=4$ |
| (d) | $\log_5 0$ | No | argument $0$: no power of $5$ is $0$ |
| (e) | $\log_4(-16)$ | No | argument negative: every power of $4$ is positive |
| (f) | $\log_{0.3}0.09$ | Yes | $2$, since $0.3^{2}=0.09$ |
| (g) | $\log_{\sqrt2}\tfrac12$ | Yes | $-2$, since $(\sqrt2)^{-2}=\tfrac12$ |
| (h) | $\log_{8}2$ | Yes | $\tfrac13$, since $8^{1/3}=2$ |
:::

::: {.workbox}
:::

#### Drill N2b — domains and rejected roots

(i) State the domain of $g(x)=\log_x\!\left(x^{2}-4\right)$ in interval notation.
(ii) Solve $\log_x 4=-2$.
(iii) Solve $\log_{x}(2x+3)=2$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(i) Answer: $(2,\infty)$.**

*List the three conditions.*

- base positive: $x>0$;
- base not $1$: $x\ne1$;
- argument positive: $x^{2}-4>0\Rightarrow x<-2$ or $x>2$.

*Intersect them.* Only $x>2$ satisfies all three; $x=1$ is already outside that range.

**(ii) Answer: $x=\tfrac12$.**

$\log_x 4=-2$ means $x^{-2}=4$, i.e. $\dfrac1{x^{2}}=4$, so $x^{2}=\tfrac14$ and $x=\pm\tfrac12$.
*A base must be positive*, so $x=-\tfrac12$ is rejected. Check: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{-2}=4$ ✓.

**(iii) Answer: $x=3$.**

$\log_x(2x+3)=2$ means $x^{2}=2x+3$, so $x^{2}-2x-3=0$ and $(x-3)(x+1)=0$.

- $x=-1$: the base would be negative — **rejected**.
- $x=3$: base $3>0$ and $\ne1$ ✓; argument $2(3)+3=9>0$ ✓; and $3^{2}=9$ ✓.
:::

::: {.workbox}
:::

### N3 · Exponential and log graphs are reflections of each other

Because $\log_a$ undoes $a^{x}$, the graph of $y=\log_a x$ is the graph of $y=a^{x}$ **reflected in the line
$y=x$**. Every point $(p,q)$ on $y=a^{x}$ becomes $(q,p)$ on $y=\log_a x$:

| On $y=a^{x}$ | On $y=\log_a x$ | Why |
|---|---|---|
| passes through $(0,1)$ | passes through $(1,0)$ | $a^{0}=1$ |
| passes through $(1,a)$ | passes through $(a,1)$ | $a^{1}=a$ |
| passes through $\left(-1,\tfrac1a\right)$ | passes through $\left(\tfrac1a,-1\right)$ | $a^{-1}=\tfrac1a$ |
| horizontal asymptote $y=0$ | vertical asymptote $x=0$ | $a^{x}>0$ always |
| domain all $x$, range $y>0$ | domain $x>0$, range all $y$ | the two swap |

What changes the **shape** is whether the base is above or below $1$:

- **$a>1$** (e.g. $a=2$): $a^{x}$ **grows**, so $\log_a x$ is **increasing**. It is negative for $0<x<1$, zero
  at $x=1$, positive for $x>1$, and plunges to $-\infty$ as $x\to0^{+}$.
- **$0<a<1$** (e.g. $a=\tfrac12$): $a^{x}$ **decays**, so $\log_a x$ is **decreasing**. It is positive for
  $0<x<1$, zero at $x=1$, negative for $x>1$, and shoots up to $+\infty$ as $x\to0^{+}$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Left: base 2 (above 1) — both curves increase. Right: base 1/2 (below 1) — both curves decrease. In each panel the log curve is the exponential reflected in y = x."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(7.4,3.7))
x=np.linspace(-3,4,400); xp=np.linspace(0.02,4,400)
for A,a,lab in [(ax[0],2,'2'),(ax[1],0.5,'1/2')]:
    A.plot(x,a**x,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label=f'y = ({lab})^x')
    A.plot(xp,np.log(xp)/np.log(a),color='crimson',lw=2,label=f'y = log_{lab} x')
    A.plot(x,x,color='0.55',ls='--',lw=1,label='y = x')
    for P in [(1,0),(a,1),(1/a,-1)]:
        A.plot(*P,'o',color='crimson',ms=4)
    A.annotate('(1, 0)',(1,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,-12),fontsize=7.5)
    A.annotate(f'({lab}, 1)',(a,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4),fontsize=7.5)
    A.annotate(f'({1/a:g}, −1)',(1/a,-1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,-12),fontsize=7.5)
    A.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6)
    A.set_xlim(-3,4); A.set_ylim(-3,4); A.set_aspect('equal'); A.grid(alpha=0.25); A.legend(fontsize=7,loc='upper left')
ax[0].set_title('a > 1: increasing',fontsize=9); ax[1].set_title('0 < a < 1: decreasing',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A base below $1$ is really the reflection of a base above $1$. By change of base,
$$\log_{1/a}x=\frac{\log_a x}{\log_a(1/a)}=\frac{\log_a x}{-1}=-\log_a x,$$
so $y=\log_{1/2}x$ is $y=\log_2 x$ **reflected in the $x$-axis**. That single fact explains every "flip" on
this page.

### N4 · The four cases for the sign of $\log_a b$

Read the sign straight off the two graphs in N3, at the point $x=b$:

| Base | Argument | Where on the graph | Sign of $\log_a b$ | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $a>1$ | $b>1$ | right of $(1,0)$ on a rising curve | **positive** | $\log_2 8=3$ |
| $a>1$ | $0<b<1$ | left of $(1,0)$ on a rising curve | **negative** | $\log_2\tfrac18=-3$ |
| $0<a<1$ | $b>1$ | right of $(1,0)$ on a falling curve | **negative** | $\log_{1/2}8=-3$ |
| $0<a<1$ | $0<b<1$ | left of $(1,0)$ on a falling curve | **positive** | $\log_{1/2}\tfrac18=3$ |

The pattern: $\log_a b$ is **positive when $a$ and $b$ are on the same side of $1$**, negative when they are
on opposite sides, and zero exactly when $b=1$. In one line,
$$\log_a b>0\iff(a-1)(b-1)>0.$$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Left: the four cases read off y = log₂x (blue) and y = log_(1/2)x (red). Right: the sign of log_a b over the (a, b) plane — positive where a and b lie on the same side of 1."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(7.6,3.6))
xp=np.linspace(0.03,4,400)
A=ax[0]
A.axvspan(0,1,color='#f3e8ff',alpha=0.6); A.axvspan(1,4,color='#e6f4ea',alpha=0.6)
A.plot(xp,np.log2(xp),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='a = 2  (a > 1)')
A.plot(xp,-np.log2(xp),color='crimson',lw=2,label='a = 1/2  (0 < a < 1)')
A.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.plot(1,0,'ko',ms=4)
A.text(0.5,2.5,'0 < b < 1',ha='center',fontsize=8); A.text(2.5,2.5,'b > 1',ha='center',fontsize=8)
A.text(3.2,1.25,'+',color='#2b6cb0',fontsize=14,fontweight='bold'); A.text(3.2,-2.0,'−',color='crimson',fontsize=14,fontweight='bold')
A.text(0.3,-2.4,'−',color='#2b6cb0',fontsize=14,fontweight='bold'); A.text(0.3,1.7,'+',color='crimson',fontsize=14,fontweight='bold')
A.set_xlim(0,4); A.set_ylim(-3,3); A.grid(alpha=0.25); A.legend(fontsize=7,loc='lower right'); A.set_xlabel('b',fontsize=8)
A.set_title('value of log_a b at x = b',fontsize=9)
B=ax[1]
B.fill_between([0,1],0,1,color='#e6f4ea'); B.fill_between([1,3],1,3,color='#e6f4ea')
B.fill_between([0,1],1,3,color='#fde8e8'); B.fill_between([1,3],0,1,color='#fde8e8')
B.axvline(1,color='k',ls='--',lw=1); B.axhline(1,color='k',lw=1.2)
for (u,v,s) in [(0.5,0.5,'+'),(2,2,'+'),(0.5,2,'−'),(2,0.5,'−')]:
    B.text(u,v,s,ha='center',va='center',fontsize=18,fontweight='bold')
B.text(1.05,2.75,'a = 1: no log',fontsize=7.5); B.text(2.0,1.07,'b = 1: log = 0',fontsize=7.5)
B.set_xlim(0,3); B.set_ylim(0,3); B.set_xlabel('base a',fontsize=8); B.set_ylabel('argument b',fontsize=8)
B.set_title('sign of log_a b',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The same graphs tell you when a log is **bigger than 1**. The curve $y=\log_a x$ reaches height $1$ at $x=a$.
So:

- for $a>1$ (rising curve), $\log_a b>1\iff b>a$;
- for $0<a<1$ (falling curve), $\log_a b>1\iff 0<b<a$.

For example $\log_2 3>1$ (since $3>2$) but $\log_3 2<1$ (since $2<3$). These two are reciprocals:
$\log_3 2=\dfrac1{\log_2 3}$.

Size questions without a calculator all reduce to one comparison against three landmarks.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Concept — reading a log's size without a calculator

Place the argument against the three landmarks of the curve: $x=\tfrac1a$ (height $-1$), $x=1$ (height $0$)
and $x=a$ (height $1$). Whether the curve rises or falls between them is decided by the base alone.
:::

#### Drill N4 — sign and size

For each log, decide its **sign** and whether it is **below $-1$, between $-1$ and $1$, or above $1$**. No
calculator.

| | Log | Sign | Size band |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_3 7$ | | |
| (b) | $\log_3 0.2$ | | |
| (c) | $\log_{0.5}7$ | | |
| (d) | $\log_{0.5}0.2$ | | |
| (e) | $\log_{0.2}0.5$ | | |
| (f) | $\log_{7}3$ | | |
| (g) | $\log_{0.4}1$ | | |
| (h) | $\log_{5}0.9$ | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

| | Log | Sign | Size band | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_3 7$ | $+$ | above $1$ | rising curve and $7>3=a$ |
| (b) | $\log_3 0.2$ | $-$ | below $-1$ | $0.2<\tfrac13$: left of the height $-1$ landmark on a rising curve |
| (c) | $\log_{0.5}7$ | $-$ | below $-1$ | falling curve; $7>\tfrac1{0.5}=2$, past the height $-1$ landmark |
| (d) | $\log_{0.5}0.2$ | $+$ | above $1$ | falling curve; $0.2<0.5=a$, so above height $1$ |
| (e) | $\log_{0.2}0.5$ | $+$ | between $0$ and $1$ | falling curve; $0.2<0.5<1$, between the height $1$ and height $0$ landmarks |
| (f) | $\log_{7}3$ | $+$ | between $0$ and $1$ | $1<3<7$ |
| (g) | $\log_{0.4}1$ | $0$ | between $-1$ and $1$ | argument $1$ always gives $0$ |
| (h) | $\log_{5}0.9$ | $-$ | between $-1$ and $0$ | $\tfrac15<0.9<1$ |

*Check (d) and (e): they are reciprocals, $\log_{0.5}0.2=\dfrac1{\log_{0.2}0.5}$, so one is above $1$ exactly
when the other is below $1$.*
:::

### N5 · How the curve changes as the base changes

All log curves pass through $(1,0)$, so the base only controls **how steeply** the curve leaves that point.
Change of base makes this exact:
$$\log_a x=\frac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 a},$$
so every log curve is $y=\log_2 x$ **stretched vertically by the factor $\dfrac1{\log_2 a}$**.

- **$a>1$ and the base gets bigger** ($2\to3\to10$): the factor $\dfrac1{\log_2 a}$ shrinks, so the curve gets
  **flatter**. For $x>1$ this means $\log_{10}x<\log_3 x<\log_2 x$. For $0<x<1$ all three are negative and the
  **order reverses**, $\log_2 x<\log_3 x<\log_{10}x$, because the flatter curve stays closer to $0$.
- **$a$ close to $1$**: $\log_2 a$ is close to $0$, the stretch factor is huge, and the curve is almost
  vertical near $x=1$.
- **$0<a<1$**: the factor is negative, so the curve is also reflected in the $x$-axis. Bases further from $1$
  ($\tfrac1{10}$ rather than $\tfrac12$) again give **flatter** curves.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Left: bases above 1 — a bigger base gives a flatter curve, and the order of the curves swaps at x = 1. Right: bases below 1 — the same family reflected in the x-axis."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(7.4,3.4))
xp=np.linspace(0.02,6,500)
cols=['#2b6cb0','#2f855a','#c05621']
for (a,lab),c in zip([(2,'2'),(3,'3'),(10,'10')],cols):
    ax[0].plot(xp,np.log(xp)/np.log(a),color=c,lw=2,label=f'log_{lab} x')
for (a,lab),c in zip([(0.5,'1/2'),(1/3,'1/3'),(0.1,'1/10')],cols):
    ax[1].plot(xp,np.log(xp)/np.log(a),color=c,lw=2,label=f'log_{lab} x')
for A in ax:
    A.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(1,color='0.6',ls=':',lw=1)
    A.plot(1,0,'ko',ms=4); A.set_xlim(0,6); A.set_ylim(-3.5,3.5); A.grid(alpha=0.25); A.legend(fontsize=7.5)
ax[0].set_title('a > 1',fontsize=9); ax[1].set_title('0 < a < 1',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The base as the variable.** Sometimes the argument is fixed and the **base** moves — e.g. "which is larger,
$\log_{0.2}3$ or $\log_{0.3}3$?". Then study $f(a)=\log_a b$ as a function of $a$, using
$$f(a)=\log_a b=\frac1{\log_b a}.$$

- **When $b>1$:** for $0<a<1$ we have $\log_b a<0$, so $f(a)<0$; for $a>1$, $f(a)>0$. There is a vertical
  asymptote at $a=1$ (where $\log_b a=0$), $f(b)=1$, and $f(a)\to0$ as $a\to\infty$ or $a\to0^{+}$. On each side
  of the asymptote $f$ is **decreasing**.
- **When $0<b<1$:** $\log_a b=-\log_a\tfrac1b$ with $\tfrac1b>1$, so the graph is the $b>1$ graph reflected in
  the $a$-axis: positive for $0<a<1$, negative for $a>1$, and **increasing** on each side of $a=1$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The base as the variable. Left: f(a) = log_a 4 (argument above 1). Right: f(a) = log_a (1/4) (argument below 1), the reflection in the a-axis. Both have a vertical asymptote at a = 1."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(7.4,3.4))
aL=np.linspace(0.02,0.97,300); aR=np.linspace(1.03,8,300)
for A,b,lab,pt in [(ax[0],4,'4',(4,1)),(ax[1],0.25,'1/4',(0.25,1))]:
    for aa in (aL,aR):
        A.plot(aa,np.log(b)/np.log(aa),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
    A.axvline(1,color='crimson',ls='--',lw=1); A.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6)
    A.plot(*pt,'o',color='crimson',ms=4); A.annotate(f'({lab}, 1)',pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(5,6),fontsize=7.5)
    A.set_xlim(0,8); A.set_ylim(-5,5); A.grid(alpha=0.25); A.set_xlabel('base a',fontsize=8)
    A.set_title(f'f(a) = log_a {lab}',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

So $\log_{0.2}3>\log_{0.3}3$: here $b=3>1$ and both bases are below $1$, where $f$ is decreasing, so the
**smaller** base gives the **larger** value. (Check: $\log_{0.2}3\approx-0.68$ and $\log_{0.3}3\approx-0.91$.)

#### Drill N5 — order without a calculator

(i) Put in increasing order: $\log_2 5,\ \log_3 5,\ \log_{1/2}5,\ \log_5 2$.
(ii) Which is larger, $\log_2\tfrac13$ or $\log_4\tfrac13$?
(iii) Which is larger, $\log_{1/3}2$ or $\log_{1/2}2$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(i) Answer: $\log_{1/2}5<\log_5 2<\log_3 5<\log_2 5$.**

- $\log_{1/2}5$: base below $1$, argument above $1$ — the only **negative** one.
- $\log_5 2$: $1<2<5$, so it lies between $0$ and $1$.
- $\log_3 5$ and $\log_2 5$: both above $1$ (since $5>3$ and $5>2$). For an argument above $1$ a **bigger base
  gives a flatter curve**, so $\log_3 5<\log_2 5$. *(Also: $2^{2}<5<2^{3}$ gives $2<\log_2 5<3$, while
  $3^{1}<5<3^{2}$ gives $1<\log_3 5<2$.)*

**(ii) Answer: $\log_4\tfrac13$ is larger.**

The argument $\tfrac13$ is below $1$, so both logs are negative, and for $0<x<1$ the flatter curve (bigger
base) is **closer to $0$**. Exactly:
$$\log_4\tfrac13=\frac{\log_2\frac13}{\log_2 4}=\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac13,$$
which is half of a negative number, so it is larger.

**(iii) Answer: $\log_{1/3}2$ is larger.**

Use $\log_{1/a}x=-\log_a x$: $\log_{1/3}2=-\log_3 2$ and $\log_{1/2}2=-1$. Since $\log_3 2<1$, we get
$-\log_3 2>-1$. So $\log_{1/3}2\approx-0.63$ beats $\log_{1/2}2=-1$.
:::

::: {.workbox}
:::

### N6 · The laws — and the conditions hiding inside them

Every law comes from a law of indices. Let $x=a^{p}$ and $y=a^{q}$, so $p=\log_a x$ and $q=\log_a y$:

| Index law | Log law |
|---|---|
| $a^{p}a^{q}=a^{p+q}$ | $\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y$ |
| $a^{p}/a^{q}=a^{p-q}$ | $\log_a\dfrac{x}{y}=\log_a x-\log_a y$ |
| $(a^{p})^{k}=a^{kp}$ | $\log_a x^{k}=k\log_a x$ |

**Change of base.** If $\log_a b=c$ then $a^{c}=b$. Take $\log_k$ of both sides: $c\log_k a=\log_k b$, so
$$\log_a b=\frac{\log_k b}{\log_k a}\quad\text{for any allowed base }k.$$
Three consequences come up again and again:
$$\log_a b=\frac1{\log_b a},\qquad \log_a b\cdot\log_b c=\log_a c,\qquad \log_{a^{n}}b^{m}=\frac{m}{n}\log_a b.$$

**The conditions matter.** Each law is only true when every log in it exists. The dangerous one is the power
law with an even power:
$$\log_2\!\left(x^{2}\right)=2\log_2\lvert x\rvert,\quad\text{not }2\log_2 x.$$
The left side exists for every $x\ne0$ (because $x^{2}>0$), but $2\log_2 x$ exists only for $x>0$. Replacing
one by the other **changes the domain** and can lose solutions. In the same way,
$\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y$ needs $x>0$ **and** $y>0$ separately: when $x=y=-2$ the left side is
$\log_a 4$ but the right side does not exist.

#### Drill N6 — true or false?

Each statement is claimed for all $x$ (and $y$) in the stated range. Mark it true or false.

| | Statement | True / False |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_3(x^{2})=2\log_3 x$ for all $x\ne0$ | |
| (b) | $\log_3(x^{2})=2\log_3 x$ for all $x>0$ | |
| (c) | $\log_2(x+y)=\log_2 x+\log_2 y$ for all $x,y>0$ | |
| (d) | $\log_4 x=\tfrac12\log_2 x$ for all $x>0$ | |
| (e) | $\log_x 8=3\log_x 2$ for all $x>0,\ x\ne1$ | |
| (f) | $(\log_2 x)^{2}=\log_2(x^{2})$ for all $x>0$ | |
| (g) | $\log_{1/3}x=-\log_3 x$ for all $x>0$ | |
| (h) | $2^{\log_2 x}=x$ for all real $x$ | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

| | Statement | True / False | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\log_3(x^{2})=2\log_3 x$, $x\ne0$ | **False** | at $x=-3$ the left side is $2$ and the right side does not exist; the correct law is $2\log_3\lvert x\rvert$ |
| (b) | same, $x>0$ | **True** | for $x>0$, $\lvert x\rvert=x$ |
| (c) | $\log_2(x+y)=\log_2 x+\log_2 y$ | **False** | there is no "sum law"; $x=y=1$ gives $1\ne0$ |
| (d) | $\log_4 x=\tfrac12\log_2 x$ | **True** | $\log_4 x=\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}=\dfrac{\log_2 x}{2}$ |
| (e) | $\log_x 8=3\log_x 2$ | **True** | $8=2^{3}$ and the power law |
| (f) | $(\log_2 x)^{2}=\log_2(x^{2})$ | **False** | $x=8$: $9\ne6$; the square is **outside** on the left (they agree only at $x=1$ and $x=4$) |
| (g) | $\log_{1/3}x=-\log_3 x$ | **True** | $\log_{1/3}x=\dfrac{\log_3 x}{\log_3\frac13}=\dfrac{\log_3 x}{-1}$ |
| (h) | $2^{\log_2 x}=x$ for all real $x$ | **False** | only for $x>0$; $\log_2 x$ does not exist for $x\le0$ |
:::

::: {.workbox}
:::

### N7 · Inequalities: which way does the sign go?

Undoing a log across an inequality is safe **only if you know whether the log is increasing or decreasing**.

- **Base $a>1$:** $\log_a$ is increasing, so bigger inputs give bigger outputs and the inequality **keeps its
  direction**: $\log_2 x<3\iff 0<x<8$.
- **Base $0<a<1$:** $\log_a$ is decreasing, so the inequality **flips**: $\log_{1/2}x<3\iff x>\tfrac18$.
- **Always** add the domain condition (argument $>0$). It often supplies one end of the answer, like the $0$ in
  $0<x<8$.

**Unknown base.** If the base contains $x$, you do not know which way to go — so **split into the two cases**
$0<x<1$ and $x>1$, solve each, and combine.

Worked example: solve $\log_x 2<1$.

- **Case $x>1$.** The base is above $1$, so the sign keeps: $2<x^{1}$, i.e. $x>2$. Combined with $x>1$: $x>2$.
- **Case $0<x<1$.** Here $\log_x 2<0$ (base below $1$, argument above $1$ — opposite sides of $1$), and every
  negative number is less than $1$. So **every** $x$ in $(0,1)$ works.

Answer: $(0,1)\cup(2,\infty)$. The common wrong answer is just $x>2$, from forgetting the second case.

#### Drill N7

Solve, giving each answer in interval notation:
(i) $\log_{1/3}(x-1)\ge-2$; &nbsp; (ii) $\log_3(2x-1)>\log_3(x+4)$; &nbsp; (iii) $\log_x 9>2$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(i) Answer: $(1,10]$.**

*Domain:* $x-1>0\Rightarrow x>1$.
*Base $\tfrac13<1$, so the sign flips:* $x-1\le\left(\tfrac13\right)^{-2}=9\Rightarrow x\le10$.
Together: $1<x\le10$.

**(ii) Answer: $(5,\infty)$.**

*Domain:* $2x-1>0$ and $x+4>0$, i.e. $x>\tfrac12$.
*Base $3>1$, so the sign keeps:* $2x-1>x+4\Rightarrow x>5$. This already satisfies the domain.

**(iii) Answer: $(1,3)$.**

- **Case $x>1$:** the sign keeps, so $9>x^{2}$, i.e. $-3<x<3$; with $x>1$: $1<x<3$.
- **Case $0<x<1$:** $\log_x 9<0$ (opposite sides of $1$), which is never $>2$. No solutions.

So $1<x<3$.
:::

::: {.workbox}
:::

# Class problems

## 1 · Existence & domain

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — the three conditions first

Before touching the equation, write $\text{base}>0$, $\text{base}\ne1$ and $\text{argument}>0$ for **every**
log. Intersect them to get the domain; any root outside it is rejected, **including a root that makes a base
equal to $1$**.
:::

### Question 1

::: {.question}
Find the domain of $f(x)=\log_{2x-1}\!\left(6+x-x^{2}\right)$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval
notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(three conditions, one of them a quadratic inequality)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — base $>0$, base $\ne1$, argument $>0$; intersect
:::

**Answer: $\left(\tfrac12,1\right)\cup(1,3)$.**

1. **Base positive:** $2x-1>0\Rightarrow x>\tfrac12$.
2. **Base not $1$:** $2x-1\ne1\Rightarrow x\ne1$.
3. **Argument positive:** $6+x-x^{2}>0$. Multiply by $-1$ (which flips the sign):
   $$x^{2}-x-6<0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-3)(x+2)<0\ \Rightarrow\ -2<x<3.$$

*Intersect.* Condition 1 cuts off everything up to $\tfrac12$; condition 3 cuts off everything from $3$; and
condition 2 punches out the single point $x=1$. The domain is $\tfrac12<x<3$ with $x\ne1$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

:::

### Question 2

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_{x-1}\!\left(x^{2}-5x+7\right)=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a root that makes the base equal to 1)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — undo the log, then test each root against base $>0$, base $\ne1$, argument $>0$
:::

**Answer: $x=4$ only.**

*Undo the log:* $\log_{x-1}(\dots)=1$ means $(x-1)^{1}=x^{2}-5x+7$. So
$$x^{2}-6x+8=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-2)(x-4)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=2\text{ or }x=4.$$

*Check each root.*

- $x=2$: the base is $2-1=1$. **A base of $1$ is not allowed** — $\log_1 1$ has no single value — so $x=2$ is
  **rejected**, even though $1^{1}=1$ looks fine.
- $x=4$: base $3$ ($>0$, $\ne1$) ✓; argument $16-20+7=3>0$ ✓; and $\log_3 3=1$ ✓.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## 2 · Signs, comparing & ordering

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — compare without a calculator

Decide the **sign** first (same side of $1$ or not), then the **size band** (compare the argument with $a$ and
$\tfrac1a$). If two logs are still tied, raise both sides to a whole-number power: $\log_a b>\tfrac{p}{q}\iff
b^{q}>a^{p}$ when $a>1$.
:::

### Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA specimen · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Using the observation that $2^{5}\approx3^{3}$, it is possible to deduce that $\log_3 2$ is approximately

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac35$ &nbsp; **B** $\tfrac23$ &nbsp; **C** $\tfrac32$ &nbsp; **D** $\tfrac53$ &nbsp;
**E** $\tfrac12$ &nbsp; **F** $2$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(take $\log_3$ of both sides)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — power law turns $2^{5}\approx3^{3}$ into $5\log_3 2\approx3$
:::

**Answer: A, $\tfrac35$.**

*Take $\log_3$ of both sides of $2^{5}\approx3^{3}$:*
$$\log_3\!\left(2^{5}\right)\approx\log_3\!\left(3^{3}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ 5\log_3 2\approx3\ \Rightarrow\ \log_3 2\approx\tfrac35.$$

*Sanity check with N4:* $1<2<3$, so $\log_3 2$ must lie between $0$ and $1$. That kills **C**, **D** and
**F** straight away. ($\log_3 2\approx0.63$.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 4

::: {.question}
Put $\;\log_2 3,\ \log_3 4,\ \log_4 5\;$ in increasing order, without a calculator.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(compare each log with a fraction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — for $a>1$, $\log_a b>\tfrac{p}{q}\iff b^{q}>a^{p}$
:::

**Answer: $\log_4 5<\log_3 4<\log_2 3$.**

All three are above $1$, so find a fraction that separates each pair.

**$\log_2 3$ against $\tfrac32$.** $\log_2 3>\tfrac32\iff 3^{2}>2^{3}\iff9>8$ ✓. So $\log_2 3>\tfrac32$.

**$\log_3 4$ against $\tfrac32$.** $\log_3 4<\tfrac32\iff 4^{2}<3^{3}\iff16<27$ ✓. So $\log_3 4<\tfrac32$.

**$\log_3 4$ against $\tfrac54$.** $\log_3 4>\tfrac54\iff 4^{4}>3^{5}\iff256>243$ ✓.

**$\log_4 5$ against $\tfrac54$.** $\log_4 5<\tfrac54\iff 5^{4}<4^{5}\iff625<1024$ ✓.

So $\log_4 5<\tfrac54<\log_3 4<\tfrac32<\log_2 3$.

*The idea behind it:* $\log_n(n+1)$ gets closer to $1$ as $n$ grows, because $n+1$ is a smaller and smaller
step above the base.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Which one of the following numbers is smallest in value?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\log_2 7$ &nbsp; **B** $\left(2^{-3}+2^{-2}\right)^{-1}$ &nbsp; **C** $2^{(\pi/3)}$ &nbsp;
**D** $\dfrac{1}{4\left(\sqrt2-1\right)^{3}}$ &nbsp; **E** $4\sin^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(compare everything with 2)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — find one option equal to a landmark, then show every other option beats it
:::

**Answer: E.**

**E** is exactly $4\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^{2}=4\cdot\tfrac12=2$. Now show each other option is **above
$2$**.

- **A:** $\log_2$ is increasing and $7>4$, so $\log_2 7>\log_2 4=2$.
- **B:** $2^{-3}+2^{-2}=\tfrac18+\tfrac28=\tfrac38$, so B $=\tfrac83>2$.
- **C:** $\tfrac{\pi}{3}>1$ and $2^{x}$ is increasing, so $2^{\pi/3}>2^{1}=2$.
- **D:** $\sqrt2-1<\tfrac12$ (since $\sqrt2<1.5$), so $\left(\sqrt2-1\right)^{3}<\tfrac18$, so
  $4\left(\sqrt2-1\right)^{3}<\tfrac12$ and D $>2$.

So E $=2$ is the smallest. *(For reference: A $\approx2.81$, B $\approx2.67$, C $\approx2.07$, D $\approx3.52$.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 6

::: {.question}
Given $0<a<1<b$, which of the following **must** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $\log_a b<0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $\log_a b<\log_b a$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $\log_a\dfrac1b>0$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the four sign cases, plus a reciprocal)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — sign rule $(a-1)(b-1)$; $\log_b a=\dfrac1{\log_a b}$
:::

**Answer: I and III only.**

- **I — true.** $a<1<b$: base and argument are on **opposite** sides of $1$, so the log is negative.
- **III — true.** $\log_a\tfrac1b=-\log_a b$, and $\log_a b<0$ by I, so this is positive. *(Or: $a<1$ and
  $\tfrac1b<1$ are on the same side of $1$.)*
- **II — not necessarily.** Let $t=\log_a b<0$. Then $\log_b a=\dfrac1t$. Is $t<\dfrac1t$? Multiply by $t^{2}>0$:
  $t^{3}<t$, i.e. $t(t^{2}-1)<0$; with $t<0$ this needs $t^{2}>1$, i.e. $t<-1$. So it depends on the numbers:
  - $a=\tfrac12,\ b=4$: $\log_a b=-2$, $\log_b a=-\tfrac12$, and $-2<-\tfrac12$ ✓;
  - $a=\tfrac12,\ b=\sqrt2$: $\log_a b=-\tfrac12$, $\log_b a=-2$, and $-\tfrac12<-2$ ✗.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following functions defined for $x>1$:
$$\mathrm{f}(x)=\log_2\!\left(\log_2\sqrt{x}\right),\qquad \mathrm{g}(x)=\log_2\!\left(\sqrt{\log_2 x}\right).$$
Which one of the following is true for **all** values of $x>1$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0\le\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)$ or $\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)\le0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $0\le\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)$ or $\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)\le0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\tfrac12\le\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)$ or $\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)\le\tfrac12$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\tfrac12\le\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)$ or $\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)\le\tfrac12$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $1\le\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)$ or $\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)\le1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $1\le\mathrm g(x)\le\mathrm f(x)$ or $\mathrm f(x)\le\mathrm g(x)\le1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(write both in terms of one quantity)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — power and product laws; let $L=\log_2(\log_2 x)$
:::

**Answer: F.**

*Rewrite each with the laws.* Since $\log_2\sqrt x=\tfrac12\log_2 x$,
$$\mathrm f(x)=\log_2\!\left(\tfrac12\log_2 x\right)=\log_2\tfrac12+\log_2(\log_2 x)=L-1.$$
And the power law applied to the square root gives
$$\mathrm g(x)=\tfrac12\log_2(\log_2 x)=\tfrac12L.$$
*(Both exist because $x>1$ makes $\log_2 x>0$.)*

*Compare.*
$$\mathrm f-\mathrm g=\tfrac12L-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm g-1=\tfrac12L-1.$$
These are the **same number**. So:

- if $L\ge2$: $\mathrm g\ge1$ and $\mathrm f-\mathrm g\ge0$, giving $1\le\mathrm g\le\mathrm f$;
- if $L\le2$: $\mathrm g\le1$ and $\mathrm f\le\mathrm g$, giving $\mathrm f\le\mathrm g\le1$.

That is option **F**. *(Check $x=16$: $L=2$, and $\mathrm f=\mathrm g=1$.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## 3 · Log graphs

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — sketch any log graph from four facts

1. **Domain / asymptote:** argument $=0$ gives the vertical asymptote.
2. **Direction:** base above $1$ rises, below $1$ falls (then apply any reflection).
3. **Two easy points:** where the argument is $1$ (height $0$) and where it equals the base (height $1$).
4. **For a variable base**, rewrite with change of base: $\log_x c=\dfrac{1}{\log_c x}$.
:::

### Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA specimen · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
Which one of the following is a sketch of the graph of $y=\log_x 2$ for $x>1$?
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,axs=plt.subplots(3,2,figsize=(7.0,7.6))
x=np.linspace(1.02,10,400); xa=np.linspace(1,2.6,200)
curves={'A':(xa,2**xa),'B':(xa,-(2**xa)),'C':(x,np.log2(x)),'D':(x,-np.log2(x)),
        'E':(x,np.clip(1/np.log2(x),None,6)),'F':(x,np.clip(-1/np.log2(x),-6,None))}
for A,(k,(xx,yy)) in zip(axs.flat,curves.items()):
    A.plot(xx,yy,color='k',lw=1.6); A.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); A.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6)
    A.set_xlim(0,10.5); A.set_ylim(-5.5,5.5); A.set_xticks(range(0,11)); A.set_yticks(range(-5,6))
    A.tick_params(labelsize=6.5); A.grid(alpha=0.2); A.set_title(k,fontsize=10,loc='left',fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the base is the variable — flip it to the argument)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_x 2=\dfrac1{\log_2 x}$, then read off the graph of a reciprocal
:::

**Answer: E.**

*Change of base:* $y=\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$. For $x>1$:

- $\log_2 x>0$, so $y>0$ — this removes **B**, **D** and **F**.
- As $x\to1^{+}$, $\log_2 x\to0^{+}$, so $y\to+\infty$: a **vertical asymptote at $x=1$** — this removes **A**
  and **C**, which start at a finite height.
- As $x$ grows, $\log_2 x$ grows, so $y$ **decreases towards $0$**.
- Check point: $x=2$ gives $y=\log_2 2=1$.

This is exactly the "base as the variable" graph from N5 with $b=2>1$, on the side $a>1$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(1.03,10,400)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.0)); plt.plot(x,1/np.log2(x),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y = log_x 2')
plt.axvline(1,color='crimson',ls='--',lw=1); plt.plot(2,1,'o',color='crimson'); plt.annotate('(2, 1)',(2,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,4),fontsize=8)
plt.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); plt.ylim(0,6); plt.xlim(0,10); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P1 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=\log_{10}x$ is translated in the positive $y$-direction by $2$ units. This translation is
equivalent to a stretch of factor $k$ parallel to the $x$-axis. What is the value of $k$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0.01$ &nbsp; **B** $\log_{10}2$ &nbsp; **C** $0.5$ &nbsp; **D** $2$ &nbsp;
**E** $\log_2 10$ &nbsp; **F** $100$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(write the $+2$ as a log, then use the product law)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $2=\log_{10}100$, so $\log_{10}x+2=\log_{10}(100x)$
:::

**Answer: A, $0.01$.**

*The translated graph is* $y=\log_{10}x+2$. Write $2=\log_{10}100$ and use the product law:
$$y=\log_{10}x+\log_{10}100=\log_{10}(100x).$$
*Replacing $x$ by $100x$* is a stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with factor $\tfrac1{100}=0.01$ ("inside does
the opposite"). So $k=0.01$.

*Check with a point:* $y=\log_{10}x$ has height $0$ at $x=1$; the new graph has height $0$ where $100x=1$,
i.e. at $x=0.01$ — the point has moved from $x=1$ to $x=0.01$, a factor of $0.01$.
:::

### Question 10

::: {.question}
Sketch $y=\log_2(x-2)+1$: state its domain, its vertical asymptote, and where it crosses the line $y=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a shifted log, base above 1)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $y=\log_2(x-2)+1$: domain, asymptote, two easy points
:::

**Answer: domain $x>2$; asymptote $x=2$; crosses $y=1$ at $x=3$ (and passes through $(4,2)$).**

- *Domain:* the argument $x-2>0$, so $x>2$; the asymptote is $x=2$.
- *Height $1$:* $\log_2(x-2)=0$ when $x-2=1$, i.e. $x=3$, giving $(3,1)$.
- *Second point:* $\log_2(x-2)=1$ when $x-2=2$, i.e. $x=4$, giving $(4,2)$.
- *Direction:* base $2>1$, so the curve rises.

It is the standard $\log_2$ curve slid $2$ right and $1$ up.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(2.02,10,500)
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0)); plt.plot(x,np.log2(x-2)+1,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.axvline(2,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1); plt.plot(3,1,'o',color='crimson'); plt.plot(4,2,'o',color='crimson')
plt.annotate('(3, 1)',(3,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-10),fontsize=8)
plt.annotate('(4, 2)',(4,2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-10),fontsize=8)
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.ylim(-3,5)
plt.title('y = log₂(x−2)+1: asymptote x = 2',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Question 11

::: {.question}
Sketch $y=\log_{1/3}(x+3)$. State its domain and asymptote, whether it is increasing or decreasing, and where
it meets each axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a shifted log with base below 1)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — base $\tfrac13<1$: the curve **falls**; it is $-\log_3(x+3)$
:::

**Answer: domain $x>-3$; asymptote $x=-3$; decreasing; meets the $x$-axis at $(-2,0)$ and the $y$-axis at
$(0,-1)$.**

- *Domain:* $x+3>0\Rightarrow x>-3$, asymptote $x=-3$.
- *Direction:* the base $\tfrac13$ is below $1$, so the curve **decreases**. As $x\to-3^{+}$ the argument
  $\to0^{+}$ and $y\to+\infty$.
- *$x$-axis:* $y=0$ when $x+3=1$, i.e. $x=-2$.
- *$y$-axis:* $x=0$ gives $\log_{1/3}3=-1$ (since $\left(\tfrac13\right)^{-1}=3$).
- *Extra point:* height $1$ where the argument equals the base: $x+3=\tfrac13$, i.e. $x=-\tfrac83$.

By N3 it is also $y=-\log_3(x+3)$: the rising curve $\log_3(x+3)$ reflected in the $x$-axis.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-2.98,6,500)
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0))
plt.plot(x,-np.log(x+3)/np.log(3),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y = log_(1/3)(x+3)')
plt.plot(x,np.log(x+3)/np.log(3),color='0.6',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y = log_3(x+3)')
plt.axvline(-3,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1)
for P,t in [((-2,0),'(−2, 0)'),((0,-1),'(0, −1)'),((-8/3,1),'(−8/3, 1)')]:
    plt.plot(*P,'o',color='crimson',ms=4); plt.annotate(t,P,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,4),fontsize=8)
plt.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); plt.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); plt.ylim(-3,4); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=7.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Question 12

::: {.question}
Contrast the graphs of $y=\log_2\!\big(x^{2}\big)$ and $y=2\log_2 x$. Are they the same curve? Give the domain
and the symmetry of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*($\log x^{2}$ is not $2\log x$ — mind the domain)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2\lvert x\rvert$ is even; $2\log_2 x$ lives only on $x>0$
:::

**Answer: they agree only for $x>0$. $y=\log_2(x^{2})$ is defined for all $x\ne0$ and is even; $y=2\log_2 x$
is defined only for $x>0$.**

The power law carries a modulus: $\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2\lvert x\rvert$.

- For $x>0$, $\lvert x\rvert=x$, so the two agree.
- For $x<0$, the left side still exists ($x^{2}>0$) but $2\log_2 x$ does not.

So $y=\log_2(x^{2})$ is symmetric in the $y$-axis with a mirror branch on $x<0$, while $y=2\log_2 x$ is only its
right half. Writing $\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2 x$ silently **drops the left branch** — and with it any solutions
that live there.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
xn=np.linspace(-8,-0.03,400); xp=np.linspace(0.03,8,400)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.0,5.6))
ax[0].plot(xn,np.log2(xn**2),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[0].plot(xp,np.log2(xp**2),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
ax[0].set_title('y = log₂(x²): even, x ≠ 0',fontsize=9)
ax[1].plot(xp,2*np.log2(xp),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[1].set_title('y = 2 log₂x: only x > 0',fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.axvline(0,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1); a.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); a.grid(alpha=0.25); a.set_ylim(-6,7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 13

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does the equation $\;\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{x}=\log_{1/16}x\;$ have? Find the
solutions that are exact rational numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a base below 1 — the curve and its reflection cross three times)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $y=a^{x}$ and $y=\log_a x$ are reflections in $y=x$; for $0<a<1$ they can meet **off** that line
:::

**Answer: three solutions; two of them are $x=\tfrac14$ and $x=\tfrac12$ (the third, $x\approx0.364$, lies on
$y=x$).**

**Try simple fractions.** With $a=\tfrac1{16}$:

- $x=\tfrac12$: $\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{1/2}=\tfrac14$, and $\log_{1/16}\tfrac12=\tfrac14$ because
  $\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{1/4}=\tfrac12$. **Equal** ✓.
- $x=\tfrac14$: $\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{1/4}=\tfrac12$, and $\log_{1/16}\tfrac14=\tfrac12$ because
  $\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{1/2}=\tfrac14$. **Equal** ✓.

**Why they come in a pair.** The two curves are reflections of each other in $y=x$, so if $(p,q)$ is a crossing
then so is $(q,p)$. Here $\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac14\right)$ and $\left(\tfrac14,\tfrac12\right)$ are that pair.

**The third one.** $y=\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{x}$ is decreasing and $y=x$ is increasing, so they cross exactly
once, at some $x=c$ with $c=\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^{c}$. That point is on $y=x$, so it lies on **both**
curves. Numerically $c\approx0.364$, which is different from $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac12$.

*The warning:* for a base **above** $1$ the two curves can only meet on $y=x$. With a base **below** $1$ they
are both decreasing and can weave across each other — so do not assume "exponential $=$ log" has at most one
solution.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.02,1.0,600); a=1/16
fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.2,6.4))
for A,lim in [(ax[0],(0,1)),(ax[1],(0.2,0.55))]:
    A.plot(x,a**x,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y = (1/16)^x')
    A.plot(x,np.log(x)/np.log(a),color='crimson',lw=2,label='y = log_(1/16) x')
    A.plot(x,x,color='0.6',ls='--',lw=1,label='y = x')
    for p in [(0.25,0.5),(0.5,0.25),(0.36425,0.36425)]: A.plot(*p,'ko',ms=4)
    A.set_xlim(*lim); A.set_ylim(*lim); A.set_aspect('equal'); A.grid(alpha=0.25); A.legend(fontsize=7.5)
ax[0].set_title('three crossings',fontsize=9); ax[1].set_title('zoomed in',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## 4 · Laws & change of base

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — one base, one letter

Move every log to **one base** with change of base, then give each log a **letter** ($X=\log x$, $Y=\log y$).
Products, quotients and powers inside the logs become sums, differences and multiples of the letters — a
linear system you can solve.
:::

### Question 14

::: {.question}
Given that $\log_2 5=a$, write **(i)** $\log_2 40$ and **(ii)** $\log_2 0.16$ in terms of $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(express one log in terms of another)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — break the argument into prime factors, then apply product / quotient / power
:::

**Answer: (i) $3+a$; (ii) $2-2a$.**

- **(i)** $40=2^{3}\times5$, so
  $$\log_2 40=\log_2 2^{3}+\log_2 5=3+a.$$
- **(ii)** $0.16=\dfrac{16}{100}=\dfrac{2^{2}}{5^{2}}$ (cancel $4$ from $\tfrac{16}{100}$ to get $\tfrac4{25}$), so
  $$\log_2 0.16=\log_2 2^{2}-\log_2 5^{2}=2-2a.$$
:::

:::

### Question 15

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2 x+\log_4 x+\log_{16}x=\dfrac74\;$ for $x>0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a tower of bases — change of base first)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — write $\log_4$ and $\log_{16}$ in base $2$
:::

**Answer: $x=2$.**

Change of base: $\log_4 x=\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}=\tfrac12\log_2 x$ and
$\log_{16}x=\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 16}=\tfrac14\log_2 x$. So
$$\Big(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14\Big)\log_2 x=\tfrac74\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac74\log_2 x=\tfrac74\ \Rightarrow\ \log_2 x=1\ \Rightarrow\ x=2.$$
:::

### Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
The numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are each greater than $1$. The following logarithms are all to the same base:
$$\log(ab^{2}c)=7,\qquad \log(a^{2}bc^{2})=11,\qquad \log(a^{2}b^{2}c^{3})=15.$$
What is this base?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a$ &nbsp; **B** $b$ &nbsp; **C** $c$ &nbsp; **D** It is possible to determine the base, but
the base is not $a$, $b$ or $c$. &nbsp; **E** There is insufficient information given to determine the base.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(three logs, three letters, one linear system)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — let $A=\log a,\ B=\log b,\ C=\log c$; whichever letter equals $1$ is the base
:::

**Answer: B.**

*Let $A=\log a$, $B=\log b$, $C=\log c$ (all to the unknown base).* The product and power laws give
$$A+2B+C=7,\qquad 2A+B+2C=11,\qquad 2A+2B+3C=15.$$

*Eliminate.* Double the first: $2A+4B+2C=14$. Subtract the second: $3B=3$, so $B=1$.
Put $B=1$ into the first and third: $A+C=5$ and $2A+3C=13$. Then $2A+2C=10$, subtract: $C=3$, and $A=2$.

*Read off the base.* $\log b=1$ means (base)$^{1}=b$, so **the base is $b$**.
*(And it is an allowed base, since $b>1$.)* Check: $a=b^{2}$, $c=b^{3}$, so $ab^{2}c=b^{7}$ ✓.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
The real numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all greater than $1$, and satisfy the equations
$$\log_x y=z\qquad\text{and}\qquad\log_y z=x.$$
Which one of the following equations for $\log_z x$ **must** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\log_z x=y$ &nbsp; **B** $\log_z x=\dfrac1y$ &nbsp; **C** $\log_z x=xy$ &nbsp;
**D** $\log_z x=\dfrac1{xy}$ &nbsp; **E** $\log_z x=xz$ &nbsp; **F** $\log_z x=\dfrac1{xz}$ &nbsp;
**G** $\log_z x=yz$ &nbsp; **H** $\log_z x=\dfrac1{yz}$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(chain the logs, then flip)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_x y\cdot\log_y z=\log_x z$ and $\log_z x=\dfrac1{\log_x z}$
:::

**Answer: F.**

*Chain rule for logs:* $\log_x z=\log_x y\cdot\log_y z$ (change $\log_y z$ to base $x$:
$\log_y z=\dfrac{\log_x z}{\log_x y}$ and multiply up). So
$$\log_x z=z\cdot x=xz.$$
*Flip it:* $\log_z x=\dfrac1{\log_x z}=\dfrac1{xz}$.

*Why the flip is legal:* $x,z>1$ so both are allowed bases and $\log_x z>0$, never $0$.

**Trap:** option **E** is $\log_x z$ itself — the right number with the base and argument the wrong way round.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## 5 · Solving log equations (domain & extraneous roots)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — solve a log equation in four moves

1. **Collect** every log with the laws until you have $\log_a(\text{expr})=\text{number}$ or $\log_a P=\log_a Q$.
2. **Undo** the log: $\log_a P=\log_a Q\Rightarrow P=Q$; $\log_a P=c\Rightarrow P=a^{c}$.
3. **Solve** the resulting (often quadratic) equation.
4. **Check the domain** — throw away any root that makes an original argument $\le0$ or a base $\le0$ or $=1$.
:::

### Question 18

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_{10}x+\log_{10}(x-3)=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a root must be rejected)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — combine to one log, undo, then test each root in the original domain
:::

**Answer: $x=5$ only.**

$$\log_{10}\big(x(x-3)\big)=1\ \Rightarrow\ x(x-3)=10\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-3x-10=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-5)(x+2)=0.$$
The original equation needs $x>0$ **and** $x-3>0$, i.e. $x>3$. So $x=-2$ is **rejected** and only $x=5$
survives.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 19

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2 x+\log_2(x+2)=3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(same trap, base 2)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — combine first, then reject
:::

**Answer: $x=2$ only.**

$$\log_2\big(x(x+2)\big)=3\ \Rightarrow\ x(x+2)=8\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}+2x-8=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x+4)(x-2)=0.$$
The domain needs $x>0$ (and $x+2>0$), so $x=-4$ is **rejected**; $x=2$.
:::

### Question 20

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_3 x+\log_x 3=\dfrac52\;$ for $x>0,\ x\ne1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a log and its reciprocal)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_x 3=\dfrac1{\log_3 x}$; substitute $u=\log_3 x$ to get $u+\tfrac1u$
:::

**Answer: $x=9$ or $x=\sqrt3$.**

By change of base $\log_x 3=\dfrac1{\log_3 x}$. Let $u=\log_3 x$ (not $0$, because $x\ne1$):
$$u+\frac1u=\frac52\ \Rightarrow\ 2u^{2}-5u+2=0\ \Rightarrow\ (2u-1)(u-2)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=\tfrac12\text{ or }2.$$
So $\log_3 x=\tfrac12\Rightarrow x=\sqrt3$, or $\log_3 x=2\Rightarrow x=9$. Both are positive and not $1$, so
both are valid bases.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 21 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2022 · Q1H</span>

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does the equation
$$\log_2\!\left(2x^{3}+7x^{2}+2x+3\right)=3\log_2(x+1)+1$$
have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(collect the right side into one log)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $3\log_2(x+1)+1=\log_2\!\big(2(x+1)^{3}\big)$, valid only for $x>-1$
:::

**Answer: $2$.**

*Collect the right side.* For $x+1>0$:
$$3\log_2(x+1)+1=\log_2(x+1)^{3}+\log_2 2=\log_2\!\big(2(x+1)^{3}\big).$$

*Drop the logs* (same base on both sides):
$$2x^{3}+7x^{2}+2x+3=2(x+1)^{3}=2x^{3}+6x^{2}+6x+2.$$
The cubes cancel, leaving $x^{2}-4x+1=0$, so $x=2\pm\sqrt3$.

*Domain check.* Both roots must satisfy $x>-1$: $2+\sqrt3\approx3.73$ ✓ and $2-\sqrt3\approx0.27$ ✓. The left
argument equals $2(x+1)^{3}>0$ automatically. So there are **two** solutions.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 22 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P1 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
Find the length of the curve with equation
$$2\log_{10}(x-y)=\log_{10}(2-2x)+\log_{10}(y+5).$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $5$ &nbsp; **B** $10$ &nbsp; **C** $15$ &nbsp; **D** $3\pi$ &nbsp; **E** $9\pi$ &nbsp;
**F** $12\pi$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the logs give a circle; the domain keeps only part of it)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — drop the logs, complete the square, then let the three domain conditions cut the circle
:::

**Answer: D, $3\pi$.**

**Step 1 — the domain.** Every argument must be positive:
$$x-y>0,\qquad 2-2x>0\ (x<1),\qquad y+5>0\ (y>-5).$$

**Step 2 — drop the logs.** Because $x-y>0$, $2\log_{10}(x-y)=\log_{10}(x-y)^{2}$. The right side is
$\log_{10}\big((2-2x)(y+5)\big)$. So
$$(x-y)^{2}=(2-2x)(y+5).$$

**Step 3 — recognise a circle.** Expand both sides:
$x^{2}-2xy+y^{2}=2y+10-2xy-10x$. The $-2xy$ cancels:
$$x^{2}+10x+y^{2}-2y-10=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x+5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=36.$$
Centre $(-5,1)$, radius $6$.

**Step 4 — which part survives?** The line $y=x$ meets the circle where $(x+5)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}=36$, i.e.
$x^{2}+4x-5=0$, so at $(1,1)$ and $(-5,-5)$. From the centre these points are in the directions $(6,0)$ and
$(0,-6)$ — at **right angles** — so the chord cuts off a **quarter** of the circle. The centre has $x<y$, so
the side $x>y$ is the small quarter-arc. On that arc $x<1$ and $y>-5$ hold automatically (the endpoints, where
they fail, are excluded anyway).

**Length** $=\tfrac14\times2\pi\times6=3\pi$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,800); X=-5+6*np.cos(t); Y=1+6*np.sin(t)
ok=(X-Y>0)&(X<1)&(Y>-5)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.4,4.4)); plt.plot(X,Y,color='0.75',lw=1.2,label='whole circle')
Xk=np.where(ok,X,np.nan); Yk=np.where(ok,Y,np.nan); plt.plot(Xk,Yk,color='crimson',lw=3,label='the curve (x > y)')
s=np.linspace(-12,3,10); plt.plot(s,s,'k--',lw=1,label='y = x')
plt.axvline(1,color='#2b6cb0',ls=':',lw=1); plt.axhline(-5,color='#2b6cb0',ls=':',lw=1)
plt.plot([-5,1,-5],[1,1,-5],'ko',ms=4)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.xlim(-12,3); plt.ylim(-6.5,8); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=7,loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}

:::

## 6 · Quadratics in $a^{x}$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — spot the hidden quadratic in $a^{x}$

Rewrite every term as a power of **one** base, so that $a^{2x}=(a^{x})^{2}$ appears. Let $u=a^{x}$, solve the
quadratic, **reject $u\le0$** (a power is always positive), then $x=\log_a u$. If only the **sum** of the
$x$-values is asked for, use $x_1+x_2=\log_a(u_1u_2)$ and the product of roots.
:::

### Question 23

::: {.question}
Solve $\;2^{2x}-5\cdot2^{x}+4=0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a quadratic in $2^{x}$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $u=2^{x}>0$; solve, keep positive $u$, then take logs
:::

**Answer: $x=0$ or $x=2$.**

Let $u=2^{x}$, so $2^{2x}=u^{2}$:
$$u^{2}-5u+4=0\ \Rightarrow\ (u-1)(u-4)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=1\text{ or }4.$$
Both are positive, so $2^{x}=1\Rightarrow x=0$ and $2^{x}=4\Rightarrow x=2$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 24 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA specimen · P1 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
Find the sum of the roots of the equation $2^{2x}-8\cdot2^{x}+15=0$. *(Give the exact value.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(substitute $u=2^{x}$ — the sum of $x$-roots is $\log_2$ of the product of $u$-roots)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $u=2^{x}$ turns it into a quadratic; $x_1+x_2=\log_2(u_1u_2)$
:::

**Answer: $\log_2 15$.**

*Let $u=2^{x}$ ($u>0$). Since $2^{2x}=(2^{x})^{2}=u^{2}$,* the equation is $u^{2}-8u+15=0$, so $u=3$ or $u=5$.
*Then $x=\log_2 3$ or $\log_2 5$, and the sum is*
$$\log_2 3+\log_2 5=\log_2(3\cdot5)=\log_2 15.$$

**Shortcut:** the product of the quadratic's roots is $15$, so the sum of the $x$-values is $\log_2 15$
without finding either root.

**Key move:** see $2^{2x}$ as $(2^{x})^{2}$. After that it is an ordinary quadratic.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 25 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P1 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
Find the sum of the real solutions of the equation $3^{x}-\bigl(\sqrt3\bigr)^{x+4}+20=0$. *(Give the exact
value.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(rewrite everything to one base, then substitute)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\sqrt3=3^{1/2}$, so set $u=3^{x/2}$
:::

**Answer: $2\log_3 20$.**

*Write both terms with base $3$:*
$$3^{x}=\bigl(3^{x/2}\bigr)^{2},\qquad \bigl(\sqrt3\bigr)^{x+4}=3^{(x+4)/2}=3^{x/2}\cdot3^{2}=9\cdot3^{x/2}.$$
Let $u=3^{x/2}$ ($u>0$): $u^{2}-9u+20=0\Rightarrow u=4\text{ or }5$ (both positive).

*Convert back:* $\tfrac{x}{2}=\log_3 u$, so $x=2\log_3 4$ or $2\log_3 5$, and
$$\text{sum}=2\log_3 4+2\log_3 5=2\log_3 20.$$
:::

:::

### Question 26 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P1 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
Find the real non-zero solution to the equation
$$\frac{2^{(9^{x})}}{8^{(3^{x})}}=\frac14.$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\log_3 2$ &nbsp; **B** $2\log_3 2$ &nbsp; **C** $1$ &nbsp; **D** $2$ &nbsp; **E** $\log_2 3$
&nbsp; **F** $2\log_2 3$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a tower of powers — make everything a power of 2, compare exponents)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — equate exponents of $2$, then a quadratic in $u=3^{x}$
:::

**Answer: A, $\log_3 2$.**

*Everything as a power of $2$:* $8^{(3^{x})}=\left(2^{3}\right)^{3^{x}}=2^{3\cdot3^{x}}$ and $\tfrac14=2^{-2}$. So
$$2^{\,9^{x}-3\cdot3^{x}}=2^{-2}\ \Rightarrow\ 9^{x}-3\cdot3^{x}=-2.$$
*Hidden quadratic:* $9^{x}=(3^{x})^{2}$. With $u=3^{x}>0$:
$$u^{2}-3u+2=0\ \Rightarrow\ (u-1)(u-2)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=1\text{ or }2.$$
$u=1$ gives $x=0$, which the question excludes ("non-zero"). $u=2$ gives $x=\log_3 2$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 27 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P1 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
$\mathrm P(x)$ and $\mathrm Q(x)$ are defined as follows:
$$\mathrm P(x)=2^{x}+4,\qquad \mathrm Q(x)=2^{(2x-2)}-2^{(x+2)}+16.$$
Find the largest value of $x$ such that $\mathrm P(x)$ and $\mathrm Q(x)$ are in the ratio $4:1$, respectively.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $5$ &nbsp; **B** $12$ &nbsp; **C** $32$ &nbsp; **D** $\log_2 3$ &nbsp; **E** $\log_2 5$ &nbsp;
**F** $\log_2 12$ &nbsp; **G** $\log_2 20$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(split the exponents, then a quadratic in $2^{x}$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $2^{2x-2}=\tfrac14(2^{x})^{2}$, $2^{x+2}=4\cdot2^{x}$
:::

**Answer: F, $\log_2 12$.**

*Split the exponents.* With $u=2^{x}$:
$$2^{2x-2}=\frac{2^{2x}}{4}=\frac{u^{2}}{4},\qquad 2^{x+2}=4u,\qquad\text{so}\quad \mathrm Q=\frac{u^{2}}{4}-4u+16.$$
*Ratio $4:1$* means $\mathrm P=4\mathrm Q$:
$$u+4=u^{2}-16u+64\ \Rightarrow\ u^{2}-17u+60=0\ \Rightarrow\ (u-5)(u-12)=0.$$
Both $u$ values are positive, giving $x=\log_2 5$ or $x=\log_2 12$. The **largest** is $\log_2 12$.

**Trap:** **B** ($12$) is the value of $u=2^{x}$, not of $x$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## 7 · Quadratics in $\log x$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — let $L=\log_a x$

First use the laws so that **only** $\log_a x$ appears: $\log_a\tfrac1x=-L$, $\log_a(x^{k})=kL$. Then solve the
polynomial in $L$ and return with $x=a^{L}$. Beware: $(\log x)^{2}$ is $L^{2}$, but $\log(x^{2})$ is $2L$.
:::

### Question 28

::: {.question}
Solve $\;(\log_2 x)^{2}-\log_2\!\big(x^{2}\big)=3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a hidden quadratic in $\log x$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — substitute $u=\log_2 x$; $\log_2(x^{2})=2u$, not $u^{2}$
:::

**Answer: $x=8$ or $x=\tfrac12$.**

The domain is $x>0$, where $\log_2(x^{2})=2\log_2 x$ (power law), **not** $(\log_2 x)^{2}$. Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$u^{2}-2u-3=0\ \Rightarrow\ (u-3)(u+1)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=3\text{ or }-1,$$
so $x=2^{3}=8$ or $x=2^{-1}=\tfrac12$. Both are positive — **both valid**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 29

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does $\;(\log_{10}x)^{2}=\log_{10}\!\big(x^{2}\big)$ have, and what are they?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(never cancel a log)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — factor instead of dividing by $\log x$
:::

**Answer: two — $x=1$ and $x=100$.**

The domain is $x>0$ (from the left side), where $\log_{10}(x^{2})=2\log_{10}x$. With $u=\log_{10}x$:
$$u^{2}=2u\ \Rightarrow\ u(u-2)=0\ \Rightarrow\ u=0\text{ or }2,$$
so $x=10^{0}=1$ or $x=10^{2}=100$.

**The trap:** dividing both sides by $u$ (i.e. "cancelling a $\log x$") loses the root $u=0$, i.e. $x=1$.
:::

### Question 30 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P1 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
Find the positive difference between the two real values of $x$ for which
$$\bigl(\log_2 x\bigr)^{4}+12\left(\log_2\tfrac1x\right)^{2}-2^{6}=0.$$
*(Give the exact value.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a quartic that is really a quadratic in $L^{2}$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_2\frac1x=-\log_2 x$, so everything is a power of $L=\log_2 x$
:::

**Answer: $\dfrac{15}{4}$.**

*Let $L=\log_2 x$.* Since $\log_2\frac1x=-L$, we have $\left(\log_2\frac1x\right)^{2}=L^{2}$, and $2^{6}=64$:
$$L^{4}+12L^{2}-64=0.$$
*This is a quadratic in $w=L^{2}$:* $w^{2}+12w-64=0\Rightarrow(w-4)(w+16)=0$. Only $w=4$ is allowed, because
$w=L^{2}\ge0$. So $L=\pm2$, i.e. $x=2^{2}=4$ or $x=2^{-2}=\tfrac14$.

The positive difference is $4-\tfrac14=\dfrac{15}{4}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 31 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P1 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
Find the sum of the real values of $x$ that satisfy the simultaneous equations
$$\log_3\bigl(xy^{2}\bigr)=1,\qquad (\log_3 x)(\log_3 y)=-3.$$
*(Give the exact value.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(substitute $a=\log_3 x,\ b=\log_3 y$ — a linear equation and a product equation)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — turn both equations into equations in $a=\log_3 x$ and $b=\log_3 y$
:::

**Answer: $\dfrac{244}{9}$** $\left(=27\tfrac19\right)$.

*Let $a=\log_3 x$, $b=\log_3 y$. Then $\log_3(xy^{2})=a+2b=1$ and $ab=-3$.* Substituting $a=1-2b$:
$$(1-2b)b=-3\ \Rightarrow\ 2b^{2}-b-3=0\ \Rightarrow\ (2b-3)(b+1)=0,$$
so $b=\tfrac32$ (giving $a=-2$) or $b=-1$ (giving $a=3$).

*Convert back:* $x=3^{a}=3^{-2}=\tfrac19$ or $x=3^{3}=27$, and the sum is $\tfrac19+27=\dfrac{244}{9}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## 8 · Simultaneous log / exponential systems

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — clear the logs or name the powers

For log equations, take them **out of log form** ($\log_a N=c\Rightarrow N=a^{c}$; $\log_a N=0\Rightarrow N=1$).
For exponential equations, let $A=a^{x}$, $B=a^{y}$ (both **positive**) and look for a linear system or a
difference of squares.
:::

### Question 32

::: {.question}
Given $\;\log_2 x+\log_2 y=5\;$ and $\;\log_2\!\dfrac{x}{y}=1$, find $x$ and $y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a linear system in disguise)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — treat $\log_2 x$ and $\log_2 y$ as the unknowns
:::

**Answer: $x=8,\ y=4$.**

Let $X=\log_2 x$, $Y=\log_2 y$. The laws give $X+Y=5$ and $X-Y=1$. Adding: $2X=6$, so $X=3$; then $Y=2$.
Hence $x=2^{3}=8$ and $y=2^{2}=4$. *(Check: $xy=32=2^{5}$ ✓, $x/y=2$ ✓.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 33 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P1 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
Given the simultaneous equations
$$\log_{10}2+\log_{10}(y-1)=2\log_{10}x,\qquad \log_{10}(y+3-3x)=0,$$
find the values of $y$. *(Give the exact values.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(clear the logs, substitute the linear one, solve a quadratic)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log N=0\Rightarrow N=1$; combine logs on each side, then eliminate
:::

**Answer: $y=7\pm3\sqrt3$.**

*Combine the first equation:* $\log_{10}\!\bigl(2(y-1)\bigr)=\log_{10}(x^{2})$, so $2(y-1)=x^{2}$.
*The second gives* $y+3-3x=1$ (since $\log_{10}N=0\Rightarrow N=1$), i.e. $y=3x-2$. Substitute:
$$2(3x-2-1)=x^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-6x+6=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=3\pm\sqrt3.$$
*Domain check:* both values of $x$ are positive, and $y-1=3x-3=3(x-1)>0$ for both, so both are valid. Then
$$y=3x-2=3(3\pm\sqrt3)-2=7\pm3\sqrt3.$$

**Key moves:** "$\log N=0\Rightarrow N=1$" for the second equation, and combining the first into a single log
on each side so the $\log$ can be dropped.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 34 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P1 Q14</span>

::: {.question}
Given the simultaneous equations
$$2^{x}+3\cdot2^{y}=3,\qquad 2^{2x}-9\cdot2^{2y}=6,$$
with solution $x=p,\ y=q$, find the value of $p-q$. *(Give the exact value.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(substitute $A=2^{x},\ B=2^{y}$ and use the difference of two squares)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $A^{2}-9B^{2}=(A-3B)(A+3B)$ turns the second equation linear
:::

**Answer: $\log_2 15$.**

*Let $A=2^{x}$, $B=2^{y}$:* $A+3B=3$ and $A^{2}-9B^{2}=6$. Factor the second:
$$(A-3B)(A+3B)=6\ \Rightarrow\ (A-3B)\cdot3=6\ \Rightarrow\ A-3B=2.$$
*Add to $A+3B=3$:* $2A=5$, so $A=\tfrac52$; then $3B=\tfrac12$, so $B=\tfrac16$. Both positive ✓.

So $p=\log_2\tfrac52$ and $q=\log_2\tfrac16$, and by the quotient law
$$p-q=\log_2\frac{5/2}{1/6}=\log_2 15.$$

**Key move:** spot $A^{2}-9B^{2}$ as a difference of two squares — it turns a nasty second equation into
the linear $A-3B=2$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 35 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q14</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following simultaneous equations, where $p$ is a real number:
$$p\,2^{x}+\log_2 y=2,\qquad 2^{x}+\log_2 y=1.$$
What is the complete range of $p$ for which these simultaneous equations have a real solution $(x,y)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $p<1$ &nbsp; **B** $p\ne1$ &nbsp; **C** $p>1$ &nbsp; **D** $p<1$ or $p>2$ &nbsp;
**E** $p\ne1$ and $p<2$ &nbsp; **F** $p>1$ and $p<2$ &nbsp; **G** $p>2$ &nbsp; **H** all real values of $p$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(eliminate the log, then remember $2^{x}>0$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — subtract to remove $\log_2 y$; the positivity of $2^{x}$ decides the range
:::

**Answer: C, $p>1$.**

*Subtract the second equation from the first:* $(p-1)2^{x}=1$.

- If $p=1$ this reads $0=1$ — **no solution**.
- Otherwise $2^{x}=\dfrac1{p-1}$. A power of $2$ is **always positive**, so we need $\dfrac1{p-1}>0$, i.e. $p>1$.

*Is $y$ then fine?* From the second equation $\log_2 y=1-2^{x}$, which is some real number, so
$y=2^{\,1-2^{x}}>0$ exists. So every $p>1$ works, and nothing else does.

**Trap:** **B** ($p\ne1$) forgets that $2^{x}$ can never be negative.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## 9 · Inequalities

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — keep or flip?

Base $>1$: keep the sign. Base between $0$ and $1$: **flip** it. Unknown base: **split into $0<x<1$ and $x>1$**.
Then intersect with the domain (argument $>0$). The same rule applies when you **take** logs of both sides of
an inequality.
:::

### Question 36

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_{1/2}x>3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a base between 0 and 1 flips the sign)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $0<a<1$: $\log_a$ is decreasing, so undoing it reverses the inequality
:::

**Answer: $\left(0,\tfrac18\right)$.**

The base $\tfrac12<1$, so $\log_{1/2}$ is **decreasing** and removing it **reverses** the sign:
$x<\left(\tfrac12\right)^{3}=\tfrac18$. With the domain $x>0$: $0<x<\tfrac18$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

---

### Question 37

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_2(x-1)<3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the domain supplies a boundary)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — an increasing-base inequality, but the argument must stay positive
:::

**Answer: $(1,9)$.**

The base $2>1$ keeps the sign: $x-1<2^{3}=8\Rightarrow x<9$. The log needs $x-1>0\Rightarrow x>1$. So $1<x<9$ —
the lower end comes from the **domain**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Question 38

::: {.question}
Solve $\;(\log_2 x)^{2}-3\log_2 x+2\le0$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a quadratic inequality in $\log x$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — substitute $u=\log_2 x$, solve the quadratic inequality, convert back
:::

**Answer: $[2,4]$.**

With $u=\log_2 x$: $u^{2}-3u+2\le0\Rightarrow(u-1)(u-2)\le0\Rightarrow1\le u\le2$. Since $\log_2$ is increasing,
$$1\le\log_2 x\le2\ \Rightarrow\ 2^{1}\le x\le2^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ 2\le x\le4.$$
:::

Working

### Question 39

::: {.question}
Solve $\;\log_x(6-x)>1$. &nbsp;&nbsp;State your answer in interval notation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(an unknown base — two cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — split into $x>1$ (keep) and $0<x<1$ (flip)
:::

**Answer: $(1,3)$.**

*Domain:* $x>0$, $x\ne1$, and $6-x>0$, i.e. $0<x<6$ with $x\ne1$. Write $1=\log_x x$.

- **Case $x>1$:** the sign keeps: $6-x>x\Rightarrow x<3$. With $x>1$: $1<x<3$.
- **Case $0<x<1$:** the sign flips: $6-x<x\Rightarrow x>3$, which contradicts $x<1$. No solutions.

So $1<x<3$. *(Check $x=2$: $\log_2 4=2>1$ ✓. Check $x=\tfrac12$: $\log_{1/2}5.5<0$, not $>1$ ✓.)*
:::

### Question 40 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following problem: *solve the inequality $\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$,
where $n$ is a positive integer.* A student produces the following argument:
$$\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** $\Rightarrow\ \log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** $\Rightarrow\ n\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)<10\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** $\Rightarrow\ n<\dfrac{10\log_{\frac12}\left(\frac1{32}\right)}{\log_{\frac12}\left(\frac14\right)}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** $\Rightarrow\ n<\dfrac{10\times5}{2}=25$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** $\Rightarrow\ 1\le n\le24$

Which step (if any) in the argument is invalid?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** There are no invalid steps; the argument is correct &nbsp; **B** Only step (I) is invalid
&nbsp; **C** Only step (II) &nbsp; **D** Only step (III) &nbsp; **E** Only step (IV) &nbsp; **F** Only step (V)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(taking a base-below-1 log must flip the sign)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\log_{1/2}$ is decreasing, so applying it reverses an inequality
:::

**Answer: B — only step (I) is invalid.**

- **(I)** applies $\log_{1/2}$ to both sides. Its base is below $1$, so it is a **decreasing** function: the
  bigger input gets the smaller output. The sign must **flip** to $>$. **Invalid.**
- **(II)** is the power law — fine.
- **(III)** divides by $\log_{1/2}\tfrac14=2$, which is **positive**, so the sign is kept — fine.
- **(IV)** uses $\log_{1/2}\tfrac1{32}=5$ and $\log_{1/2}\tfrac14=2$ — correct values.
- **(V)** correctly lists the positive integers below $25$.

*The true answer:* with the sign flipped, $n>25$, i.e. $n\ge26$. *Direct check:* $\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}=2^{-2n}$
and $\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10}=2^{-50}$; $2^{-2n}<2^{-50}\iff-2n<-50\iff n>25$.
:::

:::

## 10 · Counting solutions

::: {.callout-tip}
## Method — reduce, then count

Rewrite the equation until it is **linear or quadratic** (count with a sign or a discriminant), or until it is a
**curve meets curve** picture (count crossings). Always finish with the domain check — a root that breaks a
log's domain does not count.
:::

### Question 41

::: {.question}
The number of **positive** solutions $x$ to $\;\log_2 x=\log_2(x+a)+b\;$ (with $a,b$ non-zero real) is

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** zero if $ab<1$, or one if $ab>1$ &nbsp; **B** one if $ab<1$, or two if $ab>1$ &nbsp;
**C** one if $ab<0$, or zero if $ab>0$ &nbsp; **D** zero if $ab<0$, or one if $ab>0$ &nbsp;
**E** one if $ab<1$, or zero if $ab>1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(the parameter classic)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — quotient law $\to$ a linear equation; the sign of $ab$ decides the count
:::

**Answer: C (one if $ab<0$, zero if $ab>0$).**

**Collect the logs:** $\log_2\dfrac{x}{x+a}=b\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{x+a}=2^{b}=:k$, where $k>0$ and $k\ne1$ (since
$b\ne0$). Solving, $x=k(x+a)\Rightarrow x(1-k)=ka\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{ka}{1-k}$.

*Domain:* once $x>0$, we get $x+a=\dfrac{x}{k}>0$ automatically, so the **only** condition is $x>0$.

- $b>0\Rightarrow k>1\Rightarrow1-k<0$: need $ka<0$, i.e. $a<0$.
- $b<0\Rightarrow0<k<1\Rightarrow1-k>0$: need $ka>0$, i.e. $a>0$.

Both say $a$ and $b$ have **opposite signs** ($ab<0$) $\to$ **one** solution; $ab>0\to$ **none**.
:::

### Question 42

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does $\;\log_2 x=x-2\;$ have? Find any that are integers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(a line meets the log curve)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — count crossings of $y=\log_2 x$ and $y=x-2$ using sign changes of the difference
:::

**Answer: two solutions; $x=4$ is the integer one (the other lies between $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac12$).**

Let $d(x)=\log_2 x-(x-2)$ and look for sign changes.

| $x$ | $\tfrac14$ | $\tfrac12$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\log_2 x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| $x-2$ | $-1.75$ | $-1.5$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $2$ | $6$ |
| $d(x)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

- Between $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac12$, $d$ changes sign — one root there ($x\approx0.31$).
- At $x=4$, $d=0$ exactly: $\log_2 4=2=4-2$ ✓.

*Why no more:* the log curve bends downwards (concave), so a straight line can cross it **at most twice**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.02,8,600)
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0)); plt.plot(x,np.log2(x),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y = log₂x'); plt.plot(x,x-2,color='crimson',lw=1.6,label='y = x − 2')
plt.plot([0.3099,4],[np.log2(0.3099),2],'ko',ms=4); plt.axhline(0,color='k',lw=0.6); plt.axvline(0,color='k',lw=0.6)
plt.ylim(-4,5); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Question 43 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following equation where $a$ is a real number and $a>1$:
$$(*)\qquad a^{x}=x.$$
Which of the following equations must have the same number of real solutions as $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $\log_a x=x$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $a^{2x}=x^{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $a^{2x}=2x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(same solutions, or same count after a substitution?)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — undo the log; substitute $t=2x$; square roots bring a $\pm$
:::

**Answer: F — I and III only.**

- **I — same.** $\log_a x=x$ means exactly $a^{x}=x$ (with $x>0$, but every solution of $a^{x}=x$ is positive
  anyway, because $a^{x}>0$). Identical solution sets.
- **III — same count.** Put $t=2x$: the equation becomes $a^{t}=t$, which is $(*)$ in the letter $t$. Each
  solution $t$ gives exactly one $x=\tfrac t2$.
- **II — not the same.** $a^{2x}=x^{2}$ means $(a^{x})^{2}=x^{2}$, so $a^{x}=x$ **or** $a^{x}=-x$. The second
  equation always has exactly one solution (for $x<0$, $a^{x}$ rises from $0$ to $1$ while $-x$ falls from
  $\infty$ to $0$). So II has **one more** solution than $(*)$.

*(E.g. $a=2$: $(*)$ has no solutions, but II has one.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
